title: QuillEdge Dedicated Capacity Discovery - Decision Criteria
summary: Initial discovery focused on QuillEdge's decision criteria between Redwood Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Main themes: predictable reserved GPU throughput, tenant isolation and VPC/on-prem constraints, burst and warm-pool strategy, compliance (SOC 2 / SSO / KMS), performance vs. cost tradeoffs, and an ask for benchmark playbook. Customer leans toward Dedicated with private networking but needs clarity on failover and cost during spikes.
topics: Reserved GPU sizing and committed throughput
Tenant isolation and VPC / on-prem options
Burst strategy: warm pools, pre-warm, fallback to hosted
Security: SOC 2, SAML/SSO, KMS, audit logs
Operational runbooks: rollouts, canaries and fallback
Cost vs latency tradeoffs; quantization and batching recommendations
action_items: Maya Chen: Send Dedicated pricing tiers, committed GPU pricing, and burst cost worksheet by 2027-08-02
Liam Park: Share benchmark spreadsheet template and sample prewarm latency numbers (50/95/99) by 2027-08-03
Evan Brooks: Provide current qps and p95 token latency from prod and representative prompt mix by 2027-07-30
Sandra Lopez: Confirm compliance contact and SSO/SAML provider details by 2027-07-29
next_steps: Redwood to run a pilot on a 2-week reserved pool with synthetic spike tests
Schedule technical deep-dive with QuillEdge infra team (SE-led) week of 2027-08-09
Share security pack (SOC 2, ISO attestation, KMS integration guide)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-27 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam Park (Redwood SE), Raj Patel (CTO, QuillEdge), Sandra Lopez (SRE), Evan Brooks (Lead ML Eng)

Auto-summary: Quick overview of Redwood Dedicated offering, focus on reserved GPUs and burst/failover strategies. Customer wants clarity on isolation, VPC/private options, and real cost under burst conditions.

00:00:05 Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, and Liam our solutions engineer is here. How's everything on your side?
00:00:14 Raj: Hi Maya, thanks. We're good. Quick context, QuillEdge runs inference for a multi-tenant analytics product, heavy on long-form prompts, about 600 QPS peak but spiky, and we have regulatory customers that need strict isolation.
00:00:29 Liam: Got it. Do you want to walk through current infra first? e g what your GPU fleet looks like, whether you're cloud-first or hybrid?
00:00:38 Evan: Sure. Currently in GCP, mixed A100s and some older v100s; we front with autoscaling GKE pods. We see a lot of burst windows at end of month — like 10x baseline for 10-30 minutes. That spikes costs.
00:00:55 Sandra: And for some customers we need a VPC peering arrangement and customer-dedicated nodes, so data never touches multi-tenant stuff. That's a hard requirement for two of our enterprise accounts.
00:01:06 Maya: Excellent, that's helpful. From Redwood's side dedicated gives you reserved GPU pools with tenancy options. You can do isolated nodes per account or tenant-shared pools with fencing. We also support Private deployments if you need customer-managed control plane.
00:01:23 Raj: When you say reserved pools, is that like a monthly commit? And what happens when we spike beyond that reserve?
00:01:34 Liam: Yes, reserved is a monthly/annual commit for a specific number of GPUs. For spikes we offer burst capacity — two modes: warm pool prewarmed GPUs that are billed at a reduced burst rate, and fallback to hosted multi-tenant capacity if you have that enabled. There are also configurable policies for routing by latency or cost.
00:01:56 Evan: So the warm pool — how fast do you prewarm? What's the p95 of the first token after prewarm vs cold start? Our apps are sensitive to 99th percentile.
00:02:08 Liam: Our typical prewarm target is 30–90 seconds to hit steady KV cache. Sample numbers: first token p95 in prewarm scenario around 110–180 ms for medium-sized seqs, cold starts can be multiple seconds depending on model and quantization — though we do continuous batching which helps. I'll send the exact bench sheet.
00:02:29 Raj: That first-token number is a little higher than we hoped — our 99 needs to be under 300ms for some pathways.
00:02:37 Maya: We should be able to design prewarm+prefix caching to hit that 99 in most cases, especially if you can tolerate routing some traffic to a slightly cheaper model variant during big storms. Also quantization can reduce mem and warm time.
00:02:52 Sandra: About isolation: we have two customers that require physical isolation, or at least dedicated tenancy on the same cloud provider and their logs retained in their own KMS-managed bucket. Can Redwood do per-tenant KMS?
00:03:06 Liam: Yes, for Private or Dedicated with VPC you can integrate your KMS/HSM. We support customer-managed keys for model input and audit logs. Audit logs themselves can be exported to your GCS/S3 with separate buckets per customer.
00:03:19 Raj: And for SOC 2, do you have reports we can share with procurement? Also SSO for operator access — we use Okta.
00:03:27 Maya: We have SOC 2 Type II, ISO docs and an enterprise security pack. We support SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning with RBAC. I'll attach the security pack.
00:03:38 Evan: On routing/fallback — if we set an aggressive canary or A/B between variants, how do rollbacks work if quality drops? Do you provide regression alerts?
00:03:50 Liam: Redwood Console has rollout controls — canary percentages, automatic fallback if error rate or quality scores degrade. We also integrate with evaluation harnesses so you can tie prompt sets to alerts.
00:04:01 Raj: For pricing — committed GPUs vs burst — can you give a worked example? It's hard for our CFO to justify large commits without understanding worst-case costs during storms.
00:04:12 Maya: We'll share a burst cost worksheet that models baseline commit plus X% spike frequency and the delta if you use hosted fallback vs warm pool. It shows effective per-token cost at 95th percentile traffic.
00:04:24 Sandra: Do you support on-prem? A few of our customers are strictly air-gapped for PHI workloads.
00:04:30 Liam: We do a Private deployment option — control plane can be customer-managed in VPC or on-prem package; it requires a bit more ops runbook and usually a dedicated onboarding. We can map that path.
00:04:42 Evan: One thing we worry about is eviction or preemption if a reserved pool is on shared tenancy — what's blast radius?
00:04:50 Liam: If you choose isolated nodes per tenant, blast radius is limited. If tenant-shared, we have soft quotas and evict policies; reserved pools have guaranteed capacity while spot or shared hosts are used for burst if you allow it. We also offer preemption policies that favor fairness or priority.
00:05:06 Raj: Do you offer SLA credits for latency or availability? Our customers require 99.9 for inference endpoints.
00:05:12 Maya: Dedicated comes with SLA options — we can scope availability and p95 latency SLOs in the contract for an enterprise tier. We'll need to size the pool and region commitments.
00:05:22 Sandra: On metrics and observability — do you provide token-level breakdowns, per-route latency, and tracing hooks? We'll need to integrate with DataDog and internal tracing.
00:05:32 Liam: Console gives per-route and per-model breakdown, token cost, and tracing hooks. We have a DataDog exporter and open telemetry integrations.
00:05:41 Raj: Ok, let's talk about sizing. We said 600 QPS baseline, but that's aggregate; we have a 10x storm to 6k QPS for about 15 minutes end-of-month. The prompt lengths average 1k tokens; some are 2–3k.
00:05:56 Evan: Correct. Our current peak is mostly short but the long ones are killer. We need to simulate realistic prompt mix.
00:06:03 Liam: For sizing reserved GPUs it's helpful to provide token/sec distribution and model selection. Two approaches: commit enough GPUs for normal steady-state and rely on warm pool for spikes, or commit for a safe percentile. Each has cost tradeoffs.
00:06:17 Maya: Also layering caching — prefix caching and KV caches — can shave tokens-in-flight for chat-like flows. If you can identify stable prefixes, you can reduce effective load.
00:06:28 Sandra: We may be able to add prefix caching for the long forms. We'll have Evan pull representative prompt sets.
00:06:35 Raj: What's the process if we want a pilot? Minimum commit? Can we run a short trial with focused spike tests?
00:06:43 Maya: We typically run a 2–4 week pilot with a small reserved pool and a synthetic spike suite. The pilot includes bench runs and a small ops workshop to validate runbooks. We can start with a 4 GPU commit and scale from there based on observed throughput.
00:06:58 Evan: 4 GPUs might be too small for sustained long-form; but for the purposes of testing burst behavior it's fine. We need to be able to generate 6k QPS synthetic load to validate fallback.
00:07:09 Liam: We'll provide a load test harness and sample configurations. Also note model variants: smaller models for fallback can reduce cost but may not meet quality. You mentioned regression alerts — tie your prompt evals to the canary so you can auto-failover.
00:07:23 Raj: Another operational question: KMS keys per tenant — what's the latency implication? We use a strict KMS policy.
00:07:29 Liam: Using customer-managed KMS has a minimal effect on token latency because keys are used for encryption at rest; in-flight encryption uses session keys. There are patterns (HSM signing) that can add tens of ms, but it's usually not material for generate latency. We'll share integration notes.
00:07:44 Sandra: Also our security team requires detailed audit logs and retention controls for 7 years for some customers. Can Redwood export immutable logs to our bucket?
00:07:51 Maya: Yes, we can export audit logs and set retention on your side; immutability can be achieved with WORM settings in object storage and with the right KMS policies. We'll include that in the security pack.
00:08:04 Raj: Let's talk about cost modeling. If we commit for 95th percentile vs 75th, what delta might we be looking at?
00:08:12 Liam: Very approximate: committing to 95th percentile often means 2–3x the baseline commit (depending on burstiness). Warm pools and hosted fallback can cut effective cost by 30–60% vs committing to full 95th. We'll put numbers in the worksheet for your specific profile.
00:08:28 Evan: We also want to understand how autoscaling works for Dedicated. Is it instant? Are there cooldowns?
00:08:35 Liam: Autoscaling for Dedicated can spin new workers from warm pool in tens of seconds if prewarm is enabled. Cold provisioning from scratch is longer (minutes). You can configure cooldowns and minimum warm pool sizes to meet your p99 targets.
00:08:49 Raj: Any limitations with model types? We train some custom LLMs and want to bring them.
00:08:55 Liam: You can bring-your-own-models (BYOM) into Dedicated/Private. We support common formats and will work on onboarding toolchains. For private/on-prem there are some constraints on base images but it's doable.
00:09:06 Maya: Ok, sounds like next step is we run pilot planning. Action items we'll capture and follow up. Anything else from QuillEdge?
00:09:13 Evan: One last nit — what about upgrades and model rollouts? We need a safe path for model updates without breaking SLA.
00:09:20 Liam: Rollouts use canaries with traffic shaping; if you have strict SLOs you can pin model versions for some routes and do gradual rollouts. We also support automatic fallback to the previous version if evals fail.
00:09:33 Raj: Great. That covers it for now.
00:09:36 Maya: Thanks everyone. We'll send pricing, security pack, and bench template. Let's tentatively schedule the SE deep-dive week of 2027-08-09.
00:09:47 Sandra: Works for us. Thanks.
00:09:50 [call ends]

Notes on transcript fidelity: occasional hear-errors (SAML transcribed as "Samel", "SOC 2" as "sock two"), speaker overlaps, and filler removed in a few places to keep readability.
